sections.h2: Selling in Wilsonville across two counties
sections.html:
Wilsonville is a Clackamas County city on the south edge of the Portland metro area, with its northern section in Washington County. Interstate 5 runs through it and crosses the Willamette River on the Boone Bridge. Charbonneau, a planned community inside city limits, sits south of the river.

The county split matters the moment you list. Most parcels are billed and recorded in Clackamas County, but a house in the Washington County section follows that county’s tax dates and recording rules. Your tax statement shows which county bills your parcel, and the title officer can confirm which rules apply to your closing.

Population is 27,833 as of July 1, 2025, up from 26,664 in 2020. The median value of an owner-occupied home is $615,300, and only 49.0% of homes are owner-occupied, so a large share of the single-family houses, townhomes and condos here are rentals. Median gross rent is $1,878.

That makes two seller situations common in Wilsonville: the owner whose tenant has moved out, and the landlord holding a rental with deferred upkeep. Much of the housing was built after 1970, and buyers often weigh a resale house against new construction nearby, so condition and price need to tell a clear story.

Wilsonville is divided into several residential areas, each with its own housing mix.

  • Villebois. The largest newer neighborhood on the west side, with homes, condos, row homes, apartments and a small commercial district.
  • Charbonneau. A golf course community started in 1972, with about 3,500 residents. Its students attend Canby School District schools.
  • Old Town and the west side. Near Boones Ferry Park, with neighborhoods such as The Park at Merryfield, Montebello and Fox Chase.
  • East side. Home to Wilsonville High School, Memorial Park, the library and city offices, with neighborhoods including Canyon Creek Estates, Wilsonville Meadows and Landover.
  • Frog Pond. Master-planned land on the northeast edge, with homes under construction.

Frog Pond’s new construction competes with resale houses, so an older home elsewhere in the city often needs a plain account of its condition and a realistic price.

Three school districts touch the city. Most of Wilsonville is in the West Linn-Wilsonville School District. Charbonneau is in the Canby School District, and areas to the west are in the Sherwood School District. Buyers ask which one applies, so check your address.

Transit is unusual for a suburb. The city runs its own system, SMART, and rides within city limits are free. The WES commuter rail ends at Wilsonville Station. Mention both when you describe the location.

Owners in Clackamas County follow that county’s schedule, and owners in the Washington County section follow Washington County’s. Clackamas County’s current dates are below.

InstallmentDue dateDiscount
FirstNovember 16, 20263% for payment in full, 2% for two-thirds
SecondFebruary 16, 2027None
ThirdMay 17, 2027None

Washington County parcels use that county’s own November, February and May dates with the same 3% and 2% discounts. Value appeals go to the Property Value Appeals Board and are due by December 31 each year.

The city has urban renewal activity. Its Town Center covers more than 100 acres around Wilsonville Road and Town Center Loop, and any new urban renewal district needs voter approval under Measure 3-632. Ask the city planning office if your house sits near a project area, since nearby construction can affect showings and buyer interest.

Oregon requires a signed seller’s property disclosure statement for homes with up to four dwelling units, and the buyer gets five business days after delivery to revoke. That is set out in ORS 105.465 and 105.475.

ORS 105.470 excludes several sellers, such as lenders selling after foreclosure and court-appointed receivers, personal representatives and trustees. If your Wilsonville property is held in a trust or an estate, the exclusion may apply, and the title company can confirm. Keep records of repairs and permits, because a buyer who sees gaps may ask for time or a lower price.

Listing or cash, the sequence barely changes. Walk through it once before you talk to anyone.

  1. Look at your tax bill to see whether Clackamas or Washington County sends it.
  2. Collect permit paperwork and receipts for past work, and ask whether Oregon’s disclosure form covers you.
  3. Request a written offer, then price the same house as a listing and set the two side by side.
  4. Pick a title company to open escrow. It orders the title report and asks your lender for a payoff figure.
  5. Sign, wait for funds, and let the title company file the deed in the right county.

sections.h2: Selling a rental or a tenant-occupied house
sections.html:
Roughly every other occupied home in town is a rental, so a sitting tenant is nothing unusual here. The lease sets the pace: showings need notice, and a closing date that lands before the lease ends creates a problem. Say early whether the tenant stays, and keep the lease and rent ledger in one folder for the buyer.

An empty rental that needs work is a different story. A cash buyer who accepts the house as it stands skips the repair list. A listing buyer usually wants repairs finished or reflected in the price. Walk the unit before you decide, and write down what is broken so you can compare offers on equal terms.

Have a few documents within reach: the latest tax statement, the deed if you can find it, and your loan details so a payoff can be ordered. Trust or estate owners should add the papers that show who may sign. Permit and repair records answer a buyer’s questions before they come up.

On closing day the escrow agent splits the tax bill, pays off liens out of your proceeds, and files the deed with the county that holds your parcel. You walk away with a closing statement that shows every charge and credit, so read it line by line.

A cash purchase removes showings, mortgage approval and appraisal hurdles, and the buyer accepts the house in its present condition. That suits a landlord with a vacant unit, an heir, or someone unwilling to pay for repairs.

Ask for the offer in writing with a closing statement. Then run a listing estimate that subtracts repairs, commission, tax proration, carrying costs and the weeks a house might sit unsold. For a parcel in the Washington County section, ask the title officer which county rules govern before signing.

faqs.q: Is Wilsonville in Clackamas County or Washington County?
faqs.a: Wilsonville is mostly in Clackamas County, with its northern section in Washington County. Your tax statement shows which county bills your parcel.

faqs.q: What is the median home value in Wilsonville?
faqs.a: The estimate for owner-occupied homes is $615,300. It is a citywide survey figure, not an appraisal of any one house.

faqs.q: What share of Wilsonville homes are owner-occupied?
faqs.a: About 49.0%, so roughly half of occupied homes are rented. That is why tenant-occupied and rental sales come up often.

faqs.q: Which school district is my Wilsonville house in?
faqs.a: Most of the city is in the West Linn-Wilsonville School District. Charbonneau is in the Canby School District, and areas to the west are in the Sherwood School District.

faqs.q: When are Wilsonville property taxes due?
faqs.a: For Clackamas County parcels, the current dates are November 16, 2026, February 16, 2027 and May 17, 2027. Washington County parcels follow that county's separate November, February and May dates.
